advisor.summary: Reg. §1.469-2(f)(6) runs one direction only: net income from renting property to a business in which the taxpayer materially participates is recharacterized as non-passive, while a net loss on the same lease stays passive. The asymmetry is deliberate — it stops owners from manufacturing passive income by paying themselves rent — and Krukowski settled the regulation's validity. The planning consequences are structural: self-rental income can never absorb passive losses from other investments, and accelerated deductions on a self-rented building (a cost segregation study, a heavy repair year) strand a passive loss beside non-passive business income unless the rental and the business are grouped as one activity under Reg. §1.469-4(d). Rent-setting within arm's-length bounds and the grouping decision must precede the depreciation strategies — which is why this record is advisory: the value lies in sequencing and structure, not a computable deduction.
mechanics: The rule itself: rent property to a trade or business in which the taxpayer (or spouse) materially participates, and net rental income for the year becomes non-passive under Reg. §1.469-2(f)(6) — while a net loss stays passive; the asymmetry never nets.

The standard fix groups the rental with the operating business as one activity under Reg. §1.469-4(d) — available where ownership is proportionate or one activity is insubstantial — with the Rev. Proc. 2010-13 disclosure filed when the grouping is made.

Rent level is a genuine lever within arm’s-length bounds: lower rent leaves income in the operating business; higher rent shifts it to the rental side, where it is non-passive yet escapes self-employment tax — comparables in the file keep the choice defensible.
A self-rental to a commonly controlled business generally keeps trade-or-business status for the §199A deduction under Reg. §1.199A-1(b)(14), preserving QBI on the rental income.

Sequencing rule for the whole real-estate stack: decide the grouping before cost segregation or major repairs on a self-rented building — an ungrouped building’s accelerated loss lands in the passive bucket next to non-passive business income.

authority.note: The self-rental recharacterization itself: income non-passive, losses still passive — the asymmetry this planning works around.
Rejected a validity challenge to the regulation — an attorney renting an office building to his own firm; the rule is settled law.
Sets when a rental may be grouped with the operating business — proportionate ownership or insubstantiality — the principal structural fix.
Treats property leased to a commonly controlled business as a trade or business for QBI purposes.
Prescribes the written disclosure required when the grouping fix is elected.

requirements: A complete inventory of every arrangement in which the client or spouse rents property to an entity where they materially participate.
A written, arm’s-length lease with rent tied to market comparables.
For the grouping fix: proportionate ownership (or insubstantiality) plus a timely Rev. Proc. 2010-13 disclosure.
A rent-level review before any year in which major deductions are planned on the building.
risks: The leading audit theory treats self-rental income as passive to absorb other passive losses — precisely the position Krukowski v. Commissioner, 279 F.3d 547 (7th Cir. 2002), forecloses; exam adjusts the character, the losses re-strand, and penalties follow.
Cost segregation on an ungrouped self-rented building is the classic sequencing error: an expensive study that yields a stranded passive loss.
Rent set far from market invites recharacterization of the arrangement itself, plus collateral payroll and state scrutiny.
The grouping binds future years and reshapes loss release at disposition — model the exit before filing the disclosure.
Retirement or a role change ends material participation and flips the analysis; revisit the structure at every ownership or participation change.
stateNotes: Conformity: the recharacterization is a federal character rule that states inherit through their federal starting points — conforming states follow the federal passive-loss result.
Missouri conforms through federal AGI (RSMo §143.121); no Missouri-specific filing attaches to the grouping or the lease.
PTET interaction: rent paid by an electing operating entity deducts against its PTET base while the rental income sits outside it — re-run the PTET projection whenever the rent level is reset.
reviewChecklist: Self-rental arrangements inventoried and material participation confirmed on the operating side.
Lease in writing and current, with rent tied to retained comparables.
Grouping analysis complete and the disclosure filed where elected — before any depreciation strategy launches.
Rental’s QBI treatment confirmed under the common-control rule.
Exit and disposition consequences of any grouping modeled and documented.

client.teaser: Do you own the building your business rents? A one-way tax rule can cost you unless you plan ahead.
client.headline: Renting to your own business: stay ahead of the one-way rule
plainEnglish: Many owners hold their building in their own name and rent it to their company. That is smart for liability. But a special tax rule kicks in: if the building makes money, that profit counts as active income. If it loses money, the loss is passive — and often stuck.

This one-way rule surprises people twice. Rent income from your own company cannot soak up losses from other investments. And big spending on the building — renovations, fast depreciation — can create a loss that just sits in a bucket and does nothing.

The fixes are structural and simple. Often one election treats the building and the business as a single activity. We set the rent at a documented market rate. Done before the big deductions, the rule stops working against you.
client.analogy: It works like a one-way valve in your plumbing. We cannot remove it, but we can route the pipes so it never blocks your flow.
benefits: Keeps big building deductions usable instead of stuck
Rent set where it saves the most across the business and the building
Heads off a common and costly audit surprise
steps: WE review the lease, the ownership, and the rent level.
WE set the structure and elections so future deductions land where they count.
WE document the market rent so the setup holds up under review.
YOU sign the updated lease and keep payments flowing on its terms.
clientCommitments: Pay rent exactly as the lease says, from the business account
Tell us before major building spending or any ownership change

annualMaintenance: Review the rent level each year against current comparables
Re-confirm material participation and ownership alignment each year
Route any planned building deductions through the structure first
deliverables: Self-rental structure memo with the rent-setting analysis
Grouping election and disclosure filings where elected
